replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into ChatGPT, the model never actually sees that word.

It sees three pieces: **"un"**, **"believ"**, **"able"** — each one a number.

That's because the first thing an LLM does is break your text into **tokens** — small chunks that are the model's actual alphabet. A token is usually a word fragment, a common word, or a punctuation mark. GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of roughly 100,000 of them.

Every token gets converted to a number, and that number points to a location in a massive mathematical space.

[KEY]Tokens are the basic unit an LLM reads — not words, not letters, but learned chunks that get converted to numbers.[/KEY]

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank" becomes something like [40, 1816, 284, 262, 3331] — and the model works entirely with those numbers from this point forward.[/EX]

Here's what makes this tricky: the word "bank" could mean a riverbank or a financial institution. At the tokenization stage, the model doesn't know yet. It's just a number.

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually convert your text into before the model processes it?
A) Full sentences stored as strings
B) Numbered chunks called tokens
C) Individual letters, one at a time
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Numbered chunks called tokens
replies.raw:
That's exactly right — tokens are numbers all the way down, and the model never sees raw text at all.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers don't just sit there — each token gets placed into what's called an **embedding space**.

Think of it as a map with hundreds of dimensions. Tokens that tend to appear in similar contexts end up close together on that map. "King" and "queen" are neighbors.

"Bank" (financial) and "bank" (river) actually land in *different neighborhoods* depending on the words around them.

That's how the model starts to resolve ambiguity — not by looking up a definition, but by reading the surrounding context.

[KEY]Embeddings place each token in a high-dimensional mathematical space where meaning emerges from proximity and context.[/KEY]

[EX]In the famous Word2Vec demonstration (Google, 2013), the embedding space captured relationships so cleanly that "king" − "man" + "woman" ≈ "queen" — arithmetic on meaning.[/EX]

This is also why LLMs aren't doing a Google search when you ask them something. There's no database being looked up. It's all geometry — positions and distances in that mathematical space.

[Q]
Why does "bank" land in different locations in embedding space depending on the sentence around it?
A) The model looks it up in a dictionary to find the right meaning
B) The tokenizer assigns it a different number each time
C) Nearby tokens shift its position toward the relevant meaning
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: can we keep going with the lesson
replies.raw:
Picked C, or just ready to move on — either way, you've got the right instinct: context shapes meaning in embedding space.

Now for the part that makes everything click: **next-token prediction**.

After tokenization and embedding, the model does one job, over and over. It looks at all the tokens so far and asks: *what token is most likely to come next?*

It doesn't plan a full sentence. It doesn't reason through an answer. It picks one token, appends it, then repeats — sometimes hundreds of times to produce a single response.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by predicting one token at a time, each prediction informed by everything that came before it.[/KEY]

[EX]Given "The cat sat on the ___", the model assigns high probability to "mat", "floor", "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen". It picks from that probability distribution, not a lookup table.[/EX]

This is why AI can sound fluent and confident even when it's wrong. Fluency comes from predicting *plausible* next tokens — not *true* ones. The model is optimizing for "what fits here?"

not "what is accurate?"

That gap — plausible vs. true — is one of the most important ideas in all of AI literacy.

[Q]
What is an LLM actually doing when it generates a response?
A) Predicting the most likely next token, one at a time
B) Searching the internet for the most relevant answer
C) Retrieving the closest matching text from its training data
ANS: A
[/Q]

Now here's where it gets interesting. Once your prompt is a sequence of numbers, the model needs to figure out which tokens *matter* to each other.

This happens in parallel across dozens of "attention heads" simultaneously, each one picking up on different kinds of relationships — grammar, meaning, reference.

[EX]In "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big," attention is what lets the model figure out that "it" refers to the trophy, not the suitcase — a genuinely hard inference humans make instantly.[/EX]

A) Translating tokens back into readable words
B) Letting each token weigh how relevant other tokens are to its meaning

replies.raw:
Here's a wild fact to start: when you type the word "unbelievable" into an AI, it probably doesn't see one word — it sees **three pieces**: "un", "believ", "able."

That's because the first thing an LLM does is break your input into **tokens** — not words, not letters, but chunks that the model learned are useful during training.

A token is roughly 3–4 characters on average. GPT-4 works with a vocabulary of about 100,000 possible tokens. Common words like "the" get their own token; rare words get split into parts.

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank" becomes something like: ["I", " went", " to", " the", " bank"] — five tokens. But "tokenization" might become ["token", "ization"] — two tokens. The model never sees the original letters, only these numbered chunks.[/EX]

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into numbered chunks — tokens — before the model processes a single word of meaning.[/KEY]

Here's the thing that surprises most people: the model doesn't "read" your prompt the way you do. It receives a list of numbers. Everything that happens next — all the apparent understanding — starts from that list.

[Q]
What is a token in an LLM?
A) A single letter the model reads one at a time
B) A copy of a word the model looks up in a dictionary
C) A numbered chunk of text, roughly 3–4 characters, that the model actually processes
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) A numbered chunk of text, roughly 3–4 characters, that the model actually processes
replies.raw:
Exactly right — tokens are the model's actual unit of input, not words or letters.

Now here's where it gets interesting: once your prompt is a list of token-numbers, the model's job is to predict what comes next — one token at a time.

This is called **next-token prediction**, and it's the engine behind everything an LLM does.

The model looks at all the tokens so far and assigns a probability to every token in its vocabulary — all 100,000 of them. The highest-probability token gets picked (roughly), appended to the sequence, and then the whole process repeats for the next position.

[EX]Feed the model "The cat sat on the ___" and it assigns very high probability to tokens like "mat", "floor", "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." It's not retrieving a stored answer; it's running a probability calculation every single step.[/EX]

[KEY]Next-token prediction means the model generates text by repeatedly asking "given everything so far, what token is most likely next?" — one token at a time, not one sentence at a time.[/KEY]

This is also why AI can sound fluent and still be wrong — it's optimizing for *likely*, not *true*. But we'll dig into that in a later lesson.

[Q]
What is the model actually doing when it generates each word of a response?
A) Searching the internet for the most relevant sentence
B) Retrieving a pre-written answer from its training data
C) Calculating which token is most probable given all previous tokens
ANS: C
[/Q]
